Introduction - February 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

- **_Base metal prices have fallen sharply so far this year.  However, the correction needs to be viewed in light of last year’s advances.  GFMS believes that further downside is limited._** 

- **_Chinese imports has started to turn positive again for aluminium and copper.  For the latter, this was due to the depletion of inventories built up in the first half of last year._** 

- **_All key economic indicators are still supportive of economic recovery.  GFMS expe

ct that this will see demand growth accelerate in 2010, boosted by low downstream inventories._** - **_GFMS see the aluminium market conditions (namely higher production, higher inventories and higher prices) as unsustainable and expect prices to give up some of their recent gains._** - **_Copper has received some fundamental support from strike action and the return of Chinese buying. Supply tightness supported the market in 2009 and looks set to do the same this year, as the spate of strikes in Chile suggests labour disputes are still a feature of the market._** - **_Still no major sign of a turnaround in nickel’s fundamentals as stainless mills (outside of China) limit output to support prices._** - **_For tin, supply disruptions appear to have helped stemed the rise in LME inventories, as demand from the electronics sector improves._** - **_Zinc demand has been slow so far to respond to the early signs of a pick up in economic activity. Coupled with higher production, this perpetuates the surplus in the market._** ###### **A correction rather than a collapse** So far this year base metals have fallen sharply with the GFMS Base Metals Index having fallen by 18.8% and the LMEX down 18.4% from their respective January peaks. The correction needs to be viewed in the light of the exceptional gains seen last year rather than as a signal of a sustained correction in prices. The other key driver behind the correction in prices is the recent strengthening of the dollar. As we discussed in our previous monthly we essentially see 2010 as a year of consolidating last year’s gains. Even though prices have fallen by over 10% since the beginning of the year we still view this as the key theme in terms of pricing for 2010. - **_LME inventories for lead are the most favourable among base metals and this will likely be supportive of lead prices this year._** Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices

Independent - Informed - International **E2** Copper - February 2010 ##### **Copper** ###### **Recent developments** - **_Copper prices saw weakness from mid-January, falling to a low of $6,242/tonne on February 5. This was due to concerns over European debt and a tightening of liquidity in the Chinese economy. Prices have however since recovered some lost ground._** - **_LME stocks continue to rise, to over 540,000 tonnes at the beginning of February on relatively weak underlying demand outside of China. The recovery in Western World consumption is expected to be gradual over the year._** - **_Chinese demand has re-emerged, after a temporary lull, with refined imports rising 25% month-on-month in December. This strong performance is believed to have continued into the New Year._** - **_For the year as a whole, GFMS believes that the copper price will average $7,200/tonne on an expected improvement in demand. Given the tightness at the raw material stage, this is not expected to be met by an equivalent supply response. Our “high case” projections are also reflective of this, in addition to interest from investors being maintained._** - **_However, we noted in our previous report that, for prices to revisit the previous bull market peaks over the longer term, we believe that there has to be significant reversals of the uptrend in LME inventories._** - **_Additionally, given that prices remain so far in excess of marginal costs of production, a weakness in demand leaves considerable downside potential. This has been highlighted by the recent correction following concerns over future Chinese growth._** - **_However, reflective of the tightness in the concentrate market, TC/RC’s have been settled levels that are around 38% lower than in the previous year and around 7% down on midyear settlements._** ###### **Outlook for the next 12 months** ###### **~~GFMS’ Forecast Scenarios~~** ###### **~~Base Case, 40% Probability~~** - **_The correction in the copper market finally occurred in mid-January, tipped by the latest Chinese news. Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - February 2010 ###### **Market Outlook** GFMS are however relatively bullish that China can maintain its strong copper demand over 2010. Indeed, whilst the government will want to prevent the economy overheating, it will not want to negate the strong performance seen over the past year. Over the near term, Chinese copper product makers are relatively bullish on the prospects of an increase in demand after the Lunar New Year holidays, with March and April traditionally being the months when copper fabricators usually increase production in China. Some fabricators have noted improved orders as compared against the same period in previous years. Although providing a slightly more backward-looking indicator of consumption within China, importantly semis production rose 9.6% in December to post a new record at 888,505 tonnes. Cumulative production over 2009 totalled 8.884 million tonnes, up 18.7%. After surging to $7,685/tonne in mid January, copper saw weakness over the second half of the month on worries that China’s move to tighten liquidity would slow demand. Furthermore, a sharp decline in the euro, spurred by fears over Greece’s ability to service its debt and the health of other southern European countries, all contributed to rising risk aversion. These factors, combined with a jump in US jobless claims all contributed to a slowing of investment into the commodities sector, leading prices to a low of $6,242/ tonne in early February, 18.8% below the early January peak. Heightened investor interest in the sector had previously served to benefit the market, but its importance was recently highlighted by the severe correction experienced in the market on recent news. Indeed, until the recent collapse, the market had largely ignored the ongoing rise in inventories, with LME stocks climbing above 540,000 tonnes at the end of January. Chinese apparent consumption was up 5.5% in December despite domestic production being down on the previous months’ record, and was driven by a resurgence in imports into the country. Chinese imports of refined copper rose 25% month-on-month in December to 244,007 tonnes the latest Customs data showed. The rise was

fuelled by strong domestic prices, relative to those on the LME, and the arrival of term shipments before the end of the year. The country imported a record 3.185 million tonnes of refined copper last year, up 118.7% year-on-year. Imports may rise further over January and February as the arbitrage has window opened up once again. After spot copper premiums rose to $120130/tonne on the reopening of the arbitrage window, they did however narrow to $100/tonne in early February as the window closed. These levels are up from the 2010 contract benchmark of $85/tonne. However, with many end-users waiting for a price correction, many will see this as an opportunity to restock, despite the uncertain economic outlook. We have already seen some recovery from the aforementioned lows, with prices picking up almost 7% to $6,673/tonne in mid-February. We thus could see this as a relatively limited period of weakness, although much will depend on investors views as to the short to medium term macro view. ###### **Chinese demand remains strong despite liquidity** ###### **concerns** There have been recent concerns over future Chinese demand of late as a result of Beijing’s moves to soak up liquidity, after massive stimulus measures helped the economy to grow 8.7% over 2009. A monetary tightening is likely to have a negative effect on the Chinese construction industry, a worrying prospect given that, according to Antaike, the building sector accounted for nearly 10% of China’s real consumption of refined copper over 2009. ###### **Elsewhere consumption remains under pressure** The latest ICSG data shows global consumption falling 1% over the first ten months. This was driven by the aforementioned Chinese strength as, excluding China, the global total saw a 17.7% decline. Mine capacity utilisation averaged 79.7% in the January-October period, compared with 81.7% in the same period of 2008. On the refined side, output was down 0.1% in the first ten months as a result of tight concentrate availability. As noted in our last report, the total was driven by higher production in China and the African Copper Belt. global economic indicators have begun to pick up, demand in the OECD economies remains fragile. In a reflection of the weak und

erlying demand in Europe, premiums for Grade A cathode in-warehouse Rotterdam remain at $40-60 per tonne. Demand for copper products is expected to improve over the year, albeit at a gradual rate. 

Furthermore, in the US, housing starts fell 4% month-onmonth in December to an annual rate of 557,000 according to the US Census Bureau, indicating that construction demand for copper products remains sluggish. Building permits did however jump 10.9% month-on-month to 653,000 in December. 

In Zambia, a rise in output at the country’s mines has led the central bank to raise its 2009 copper output forecast to 692,604 tonnes from the previous estimate of 664,000 tonnes.  Going forward, it expects to achieve its highest copper output in almost 40 years this year, of 750,000 tonnes and is well on track for a million tonnes by 2012. This higher production will be assisted by the new Konkola Deep Mining project, located in the heart of the Copper Belt in addition to increased production from Equinox Minerals’ Lumwana copper mine over 2010.  It hopes to boost output at Lumwana by 23% to 135,000 tonnes of copper in concentrate.  Quarterly output increased through 2009, reaching 34,626 tonnes in the fourth quarter compared with 28,111 tonnes in the third quarter after the mine commenced commercial production in April 2009. 

In Japan, output of rolled copper products rose to 68,006 tonnes in December on a seasonally adjusted basis, up 17.1% from a year earlier according to the Japan Copper and Brass Association.  This was compared against a very low base last year when the global economic crisis forced manufacturers to cut production. However, this figure was representative of a 1.4% fall from the previous month. 

Furthermore, the negative state of the Japanese construction sector is highlighted by the fact that 2009 copper wire and cable shipments were believed to have fallen to their lowest level in over 30 years, at 649,074 tonnes.  The country’s consumption of copper is however believed to have now recovered to about 80% of the typical level according to industry officials, driven by relatively strong demand from the electronics sector, although the construction sector continues to show weakness. This is highlighted by the fact that December shipments fell 2.4% year-on-year and 4.2% from November to an estimated 56,300 tonnes. 

In China, cumulative mine production was up 4.7% yearon-year over the full year 2009.  After running at record levels of over 90,000 tpm over September-November, output dipped slightly in December to 80,751 tonnes.  In line with a tightening concentrate market over December, Chinese refined production dipped from the previous highs in December, to 391,306 tonnes.  This came after output hit its fourth consecutive monthly record in November, at 405,257 tonnes, after running at a rate of under 350,000 tpm over the first half of 2009.  For the year as a whole, cumulative Chinese production was up 8.7% at 4.110 million tonnes.

Southern Copper, a unit of Grupo Mexico, operates the giant Cananea mine in Mexico, which historically has produced some 20% of the company’s copper output and has been hit by a strike for the past two years. It made a fresh offer to unionized workers in late January, although the union said miners would refuse to accept it. The company’s 2010 copper forecast does not include potential output from Cananea. Furthermore, further start-up problems at Inmet’s Las Cruces mine in Spain forced it to miss its 2009 output target producing 83,600 tonnes of copper during the year. The company failed to achieve commercial production at Las Cruces during the fourth quarter, producing just 3,300 tonnes of copper cathode at the mine during Q4 as against its estimate of 8,700 tonnes. A number of equipment failures and operational issues delayed the ramp-up of the plant, and the company now forecasts that commercial production will be achieved in May. ###### **Tight concentrate market driving down TC/RC’s** We have noted in previous reports that concentrate tightness has restricted the growth in refined output in 2009. Consequently, whilst we acknowledge that uncertainty over the extent of the economic recovery may continue to weigh on prices over the very short term, over the medium to long term we expect to see copper show strong performance. Prices breached $15,000/tonne in early December, but rebounded in line with developments elsewhere in the complex and ended the year trading around $19,000/tonne. Prices remained strong until mid-January, before profit taking amidst a general bout of liquidation pushed prices lower towards $17,000/ tonne. Prices have however recently recovered back towards $18,000/tonne in line with an uptick across the complex. The extent to which technical factors contributed to the market’s recent gyrations is a moot point, but it seems certain that we saw a growing awareness that its fundamentals were deteriorating and this has contributed to negative sentiment. Indeed, it can be argued that, with the possible exception of aluminium, nickel’s fundamentals are the worst of all the LME-traded metals. This weakness was reflected in the substantial accumulation of visible stocks. LME stocks increased by 42,090 tonnes during the first nine months of last year, to stand at 120,912 tonnes at the end of September. The pace of increase slowed thereafter, but the trend remained upwards and a surge in December saw them end the year totalling 158,424 tonnes. During January, they rose by a further 7,446 tonnes to stand at 165,870 tonnes at the end of the month. ###### **Support from lower production to ease** The aforementioned accumulation in stocks occurred despite a significant decline in production, which resulted from the closure of around 200,000 tpy of capacity since mid-2008. Production was also constrained by strike action in Canada. The impact of this latter development appears certain to diminish this year and output will be boosted further by new capacity coming onstream. Latest reports tell us that production is rising in Canada. More than 3,100 workers went on strike at Vale’s operations in Sudbury and Port Colborne facilities last July and at its Voisey’s Bay mine in Labrador in August. In early February, the company announced that it intended to restart one of its nickel mines and boost production of another at its Sudbury complex in Ontario despite the seven-month strike. The company will restart its Creighton mine and operate it at full capacity, and will also raise its Coleman mine, which has been partially operational since last October, to full operation. The Garson mine has also been running at partial output sine October

. Ore from these mines will be processed at Vale’s Copper Cliff smelter, which has been operating at 50% of capacity using non-unionised labour and stockpiled feed. Elsewhere in Canada, Xstrata announced that it had averted a strike at its Sudbury operations, when it reached an agreement with unionised workers on the first day of February. The deal included the restart of the company’s Fraser mine in Ontario, where operations had been suspended a year earlier because of low nickel prices. ###### **Hopes of a significant pick up in stainless demand are limited** The global imbalance was exacerbated by the fact that demand weakened over the past two years. We estimate that global consumption fell by 4.8% last year having already declined by 4.3% in 2008. Independent - Informed - International **N3** Nickel & Cobalt - February 2010 ###### **Market Outlook** Overall, it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the global nickel market will remain in surplus for the foreseeable future. The International Nickel Study Group (INSG) forecast in November, at its latest twice-yearly meeting, that the market would be in surplus to the tune of 70,000 tonnes in 2009 and by 90,000 tonnes in 2010. Our own estimate is not as drastic, but we still believe the market was in a 53,000 tonne surplus in 2009, declining to a 23,000 tonne surplus this year on a sharp recovery in demand. We believe that, with demand remaining weak and production looking set to c

ontinue its upward trend, price gains will be restricted over the first half.  Going forward, a swing to deficit is forecast for the third and fourth quarters 

as stainless markets in the mature economies reclaim their previous losses and emerging economies continue growing, in particular China. Also, on the supply side, we have accounted for the uncertainty concerning the next generation of HPAL projects and delays at some new capacities. Nevertheless, the fourth quarter is expected to register a deficit of just 5,000 tonnes given the onset of the 60,000 tonne per year Goro project. 

As prices have remained within our ranges, we are retaining our Q1 forecast of $18,000/tonne.  Further forward, average prices of $20,000/tonne in Q4 are expected to support an average 2010 price of $18,815/tonne.

After seeing a slight deficit in 2009, we expect the market to remain in deficit in 2010 as a sharp rebound in demand outweighs the supply of metal to the market. The market will however have to absorb a number of additions to production, including the commissioning of Goro, and a number of other large scale projects further down the line. For 2010 as a whole, we forecast an average price for 99.8% of $24/lb. In terms of alternative scenarios, we believe that there is greater upside than downside from current levels. The introduction of trading on the LME should provide a boost given the influence of funds elsewhere in base metals sector. Also there are big question marks concerning the timing about the new projects that are coming onstream, both the HPAL projects and those in the African cobalt-belt. Under high case scenario, prices could average $30/lb in the final quarter of 2010. The downside should be fairly limited given that stocks are currently low. On a quarterly average basis, GFMS does not expect prices to fall below $17/lb next year. As demand recovers through the year, GFMS forecast the quarterly average to peak at around $26/lb in the third quarter.
